vignette: He is fifty-three now, though his body still carries the architecture of forty-two days spent in a windowless storage container in the highlands. He describes the event the same way each time he brings it forward: the weight of the concrete floor against his cheek, the slit of gray light above the door, the count of his own breaths when the shouting grows too loud. He travels for a photo documentary when the road turns, when the guards take his camera bag and leave him with nothing but the slow drip of condensation on the wall. He tells me that the silence is the heaviest thing he carries out. When he finally walks back into the sunlight, his wife meets him at the airport with paper cups of coffee and a blanket. She holds his hands, but he pulls back at the sudden warmth, his pulse jumping to his throat. For months, he keeps his camera on the highest shelf of the garage. He tells himself it is a broken lens, but the truth lives in the way his chest tightens when a ceiling fan cycles on, or when a heavy truck rumbles past his driveway. He begins photographing again, but only in places with wide horizons. He composes his frames with rigid geometry, aligning vanishing points, balancing exposure, as if control could be built into a grid. At home, the rooms feel too exposed. He moves through them with his shoulders hunched, eyes tracking doorways, windows, the spaces between furniture. His wife leaves steaming mugs on the kitchen counter; he drinks them cold because the heat reminds him of the plastic canteen they give him in the dark. She asks if he wants to take their son to visit her family in Auckland next season. He says yes, then spends three days rehearsing how to explain why he cannot sleep with the curtains drawn. He has stopped developing prints. Instead, he arranges his digital archives into folders named after coordinates and dates, as though mapping a route out of something he still cannot name. He notices everything. The way a shadow falls across a floorboard. The exact pitch of a siren. The tension in a friend’s jaw when they laugh too loudly. He tells me that his mind used to be a darkroom where he could soften what needed softening and sharpen what needed clarity. Now the chemicals have dried up. What remains is a raw negative, exposed to too much light. He catches himself staring at his wife while she reads on the couch, measuring the distance between them in inches, wondering if proximity ever feels safe or if it only means there is nowhere left to run. His ancestors navigated by the stars; he feels unmoored even in broad daylight. Yesterday, he brought a print to the session. It is a photograph of the Pacific Ocean, taken at dawn. The water is still, the sky bruised purple and gold, and in the lower right corner, barely visible, a single piece of driftwood rests on the sand. He says he walks for an hour to find the right vantage point. He does not tell me that he checks the exits of the park, that he sits with his back to a concrete wall, or that he keeps one eye on the path while his other lens captures the light. The image is quiet. It does not ask for anything. He leaves it on the coffee table when he goes to the restroom, and when he returns, he does not look at it. He watches the dust settle in the afternoon sun, breathing slowly, counting the seconds between the tick of the wall clock.
